23 Library: web-easy🔗

 (include-lib web-easy)

 Compile option:  --ffi --browser --ffi dom --ffi standard --ffi js

23.1 About web-easy🔗

The web-easy library is a declarative UI library for WebRacket.

The library is inspired by gui-easy, whose goal is to simplify the construction of user interfaces in Racket. The approach is to wrap the existing imperative GUI API in a functional shell and use observables to manage state.

This library follows the same approach, but the underlying GUI toolkit is provided by the browser. Due to the rich design possibilities on the web, the set of available components is larger. The intended core-vs-library split is described in lib/web-easy/API-LAYERS.md.

23.2 Quickstart🔗

The following program fragments focus on the how view and observables are used to create user interfaces. To see how the fragments are turned into a runnable program, look at the examples/ subfolder of the web-easy library. Each program in this Quickstart has its own folder.

https://github.com/soegaard/webracket/tree/main/lib/web-easy/examples

The examples are heavily inspired by the gui-easy Quickstart.

23.2.1 JSXGraph Examples🔗

The examples/jsx-graph-gallery/ folder contains the JSXGraph gallery used to exercise the wrapper classes in separate boards and stress the browser bridge.

23.2.2 Hello World🔗

Ⓦ History of Hello World

We begin with a Hello World program.

The simplest version is:

#lang webracket
(define hello-world-app-1
(window
 (h1 "Hello World")
 (text "Have a nice day.")))

The components window, h1 and text build a description of how the view should look like. The view is rendered to the browser DOM with the help of render.

When rendered, the contents of window will fill the entire browser window. Thus the header and text have no side margins.

To restrict the width, we can put the contents in a container.

#lang webracket
(define hello-world-app-2
(window
 (container
  (h1 "Hello World")
  (text "Have a nice day."))))

The container component uses these settings as default:

.we-container{
  width:     min(1200px, calc(100vw - 28px));
  max-width: 1200px;
  margin:    0 auto;
}
.we-container{ width: min(1200px, calc(100vw - 28px)); max-width: 1200px; margin: 0 auto; }

The rules imply that the width on large screens is 1200px. On small screens the size is the viewport minus 28px, thus giving a margin of 14px on both sides. The margin: 0 auto; centers the block horizontally.

The default rules can be overruled by inline styles or by using an extra style sheet. Let’s see how the #:attrs keyword argument can be used to add an inline style. Here we are changing the color of the text.

Currently our poor-man’s keyword arguments need to be last in a call.

#lang webracket
(define hello-world-app-3
(window
 (container
(h1 "Hello World")
(text "Have a nice day."
      #:attrs '((style "color: red;"))))))

Similarly, we can change the default width for a container.

#lang webracket
(define my-container-style
"  width: min(600px, calc(100vw - 28px));")
 
(define hello-world-app-4
(window
 (container
(h1 "Hello World")
(text "Have a nice day.")
#:attrs `((style ,my-container-style)))))

23.2.3 A Single Counter🔗

The Hello World programs have a static view, nothing changes. Usually programs have state that changes - and as a result the user interface needs to update reflecting these changes.

In web-easy state is represented via observables.

#lang webracket
(define @count (@ 0))
 
(define a-single-counter-app
(window
 (container
  (h1 "A Single Counter")
  (hpanel
   (button "-" (λ () (@count . <~ . sub1)))
   (text (@count . ~> . number->string))
   (button "+" (λ () (@count . <~ . add1)))))))

The counter state is stored in a new observable (@ 0). By convention names for observables like @count begins with an @.

The view (text (~> @count number->string)) depends on the observable value. If the value changes, the text is recomputed.

The minus button has the on-click callback (<~ @count sub1). This updates the observable value.

When an observable is updated, any dependencies are recomputed. Here the text is recomputed.

To sum up, ~> is used to read (and map) the value of an observable, and <~ is used to update. As an alternative to these short names, one can use obs-map and obs-update!.

#lang webracket
(define @count (@ 0))
 
(define a-single-counter-app-2
(window
 (container
  (h1 "A Single Counter - 2")
  (hpanel
   (button "-" (λ () (obs-update! @count sub1)))
   (text (obs-map @count number->string))
   (button "+" (λ () (obs-update! @count add1)))))))

23.2.4 Multiple Counters🔗

Converting a single counter into a reusable counter component is straight forward.

#lang webracket
(define (counter @count action)
(hpanel
 (button "-" (λ () (action sub1)))
 (text (@count . ~> . number->string))
 (button "+" (λ () (action add1)))))
 
(define @counter-1 (@ 0))
(define @counter-2 (@ 0))
 
(define multiple-counters-app
(window
 (container
  (h1 "Two Counters")
  (vpanel
   (counter @counter-1 (λ (proc) (@counter-1 . <~ . proc)))
   (counter @counter-2 (λ (proc) (@counter-2 . <~ . proc)))))))

23.2.5 Dynamic Counters🔗

#lang webracket
(define @counters (@ '((0 . 0))))
 
(define (append-counter counts)
(define next-id (add1 (apply max -1 (map car counts))))
(append counts `((,next-id . 0))))
 
(define (update-count counts k proc)
(for/list ([entry (in-list counts)])
(if (equal? (car entry) k)
    (cons k (proc (cdr entry)))
    entry)))
 
(define (counter @count action)
(hpanel
 (button "-" (λ () (action sub1)))
 (text (@count . ~> . number->string))
 (button "+" (λ () (action add1)))))
 
(define dynamic-counters-app
(window
 (container
  (h1 " Counters")
  (vpanel
   (hpanel
    (button "Add counter"
            (λ () (@counters . <~ . append-counter))))
(list-view @counters
           (λ (k @entry)
       (counter (@entry . ~> . cdr)
                (λ (proc)
                  (@counters . <~ . (λ (counts)
                                        (update-count counts k proc))))))
     car)))))

23.3 Observables🔗

Observables are the state layer in web-easy. An observable holds a current value, can be updated, and can notify dependent views or callbacks when the value changes.

The Quickstart examples use the short operator forms:

  • (@ v) creates an observable

  • (~> o f) reads/maps the current value through f

  • (<~ o f) updates the current value with f

  • (:= o v) replaces the current value with v

The corresponding procedure forms are documented below.

procedure

(obs? v) → boolean?

  v : any/c
Check whether v is an observable.

procedure

(obs v [name derived?]) → observable?

  v : any/c
  name : symbol? = 'anon
  derived? : boolean? = #f
Create an observable holding v.

The optional name is used for debugging and error reporting. If derived? is true, the observable is derived/read-only and cannot be updated with obs-update! or obs-set!.

procedure

(obs-name o) → symbol?

  o : observable?
Return the name attached to o.

procedure

(obs-peek o) → any/c

  o : observable?
Return the current value of o.

procedure

(obs-observe! o f) → void?

  o : observable?
  f : procedure?
Register f to be called whenever o changes.

The callback receives the new value of o.

procedure

(obs-unobserve! o f) → void?

  o : observable?
  f : procedure?
Remove the observer f from o.

procedure

(obs-update! o f) → any/c

  o : observable?
  f : procedure?
Update o by applying f to its current value. The result becomes the new current value and is returned.

procedure

(obs-set! o v) → void?

  o : observable?
  v : any/c
Replace the current value of o with v.

procedure

(obs-map o f) → observable?

  o : observable?
  f : procedure?
Create a derived observable whose value is (f (obs-peek o)).

procedure

(obs-combine f o ...) → observable?

  f : procedure?
  o : observable?
Create a derived observable by applying f to the current values of one or more observables.

For example, this produces an observable whose value is always a list of the current values of three source observables:

#lang webracket
(obs-combine list @circles @selected-circle @diam)

procedure

(obs-filter o pred [default]) → observable?

  o : observable?
  pred : procedure?
  default : any/c = #f
Create a derived observable that only updates when pred accepts the new value.

If the initial value does not satisfy pred, the derived observable starts with default.

syntax

(obs-watch! o ... f)

Observe several observables at once and call f with their current values.

obs-watch! is shorthand for combining the source observables with list and then observing the combined result. The callback f is called with one argument per observable, in the same order as the observable arguments.

Example:

#lang webracket
(obs-watch! @circles @selected-circle @diam
(λ (circles selected-circle diam)
(redraw-canvas! circles)))

This is equivalent to:

#lang webracket
(obs-observe! (obs-combine list @circles @selected-circle @diam)
(λ (state)
(match state
[(list circles selected-circle diam)
 (redraw-canvas! circles)])))

23.4 Common Keywords and Contracts🔗

Most concrete component constructors support:

  • #:id to set the root DOM id

  • #:class to add one or more CSS classes

  • #:attrs to add root DOM attributes

Composition forms such as window, vpanel, and hpanel keep positional-only contracts.

Primitive HTML element constructors also support a Phase 1 set of generic bubbling DOM event keywords:

  • #:on-click, #:on-doubleclick, #:on-contextmenu

  • #:on-copy, #:on-cut, #:on-paste

  • #:on-compositionstart, #:on-compositionupdate, #:on-compositionend

  • #:on-keydown, #:on-keyup

  • #:on-focus, #:on-blur, #:on-focusin, #:on-focusout

  • #:on-input, #:on-change, #:on-beforeinput, #:on-submit, #:on-reset, #:on-invalid

  • #:on-wheel, #:on-scroll

  • #:on-drag, #:on-dragstart, #:on-dragend, #:on-dragenter, #:on-dragleave, #:on-dragover, #:on-drop

  • #:on-touchstart, #:on-touchmove, #:on-touchend, #:on-touchcancel

  • #:on-load, #:on-error, #:on-abort, #:on-loadeddata, #:on-loadedmetadata

  • #:on-canplay, #:on-canplaythrough, #:on-play, #:on-playing, #:on-pause, #:on-ended, #:on-timeupdate, #:on-volumechange

  • #:on-animationstart, #:on-animationend, #:on-animationiteration, #:on-transitionend

  • #:on-mousedown, #:on-mousemove, #:on-mouseup

  • #:on-mouseenter, #:on-mouseleave, #:on-mouseover, #:on-mouseout

  • #:on-pointerdown, #:on-pointermove, #:on-pointerup

  • #:on-pointerenter, #:on-pointerleave, #:on-pointerover, #:on-pointerout, #:on-pointercancel

  • #:on-gotpointercapture, #:on-lostpointercapture

These keywords are part of the core primitive surface. Each callback receives the raw browser event object, so handlers can read fields such as offsetX, offsetY, clientX, and clientY.

Example:

#lang webracket
(Input #:on-keydown
(lambda (evt)
(define key (js-ref evt "key"))
(js-log key)))

value

html-attr-entry/c : 
(or/c (cons/c symbol? any/c)
      (list/c symbol? any/c))
Contract alias for one attribute entry used in #:attrs.

An entry is either:

  • a pair such as (cons 'id "hero")

  • a 2-element list such as '(id "hero")

value

html-attrs/c : 
(or/c #f
      (listof html-attr-entry/c))
Contract alias for attribute lists accepted by #:attrs.

value

content/c : 
(or/c string?
      view?
      observable?)
Public-facing contract alias for primitive element content that may be:

  • a string

  • a child view

  • an observable whose current value is a string or a view

value

text-content/c : any/c

Predicate for values accepted by text-bearing constructors: strings, symbols, numbers, booleans, characters, or observables whose current value is one of those.

23.5 Event Handling🔗

The following thin convenience wrappers are available on top of the raw event object passed to primitive #:on-* callbacks:

Example:

#lang webracket
(Canvas #:on-contextmenu
        (lambda (evt)
(prevent-default! evt)
(define x (mouse-event-offset-x evt))
(define y (mouse-event-offset-y evt))
(js-log (format "menu at (~a, ~a)" x y))))

  • #:ref on primitive elements

  • event?, mouse-event?, keyboard-event?

  • pointer-event?, focus-event?, input-event?, submit-event?, touch-event?, wheel-event?

  • touch-list?, touch?

  • event-type, event-target, event-current-target

  • prevent-default!, stop-propagation!, stop-immediate-propagation!

  • mouse-event-offset-x, mouse-event-offset-y

  • mouse-event-client-x, mouse-event-client-y

  • mouse-event-page-x, mouse-event-page-y

  • mouse-event-screen-x, mouse-event-screen-y

  • mouse-event-button, mouse-event-buttons

  • mouse-event-alt-key?, mouse-event-ctrl-key?, mouse-event-meta-key?, mouse-event-shift-key?

  • keyboard-event-key, keyboard-event-code

  • keyboard-event-alt-key?, keyboard-event-ctrl-key?, keyboard-event-meta-key?, keyboard-event-shift-key?, keyboard-event-repeat?

  • touch-event-touches, touch-event-target-touches, touch-event-changed-touches

  • touch-list-length, touch-list-ref

  • touch-identifier, touch-client-x, touch-client-y

  • touch-page-x, touch-page-y, touch-screen-x, touch-screen-y

23.5.1 Ref🔗

Primitive elements also accept a #:ref keyword argument. The value of #:ref must be an observable.

A ref observable holds:

  • #f before the element is mounted

  • the current DOM node while the element is mounted

  • #f again after the renderer is destroyed

This gives web-easy an imperative escape hatch without introducing a separate ref type. A ref is simply an observable used to track the current node.

Refs are most useful when you need to reach out from the declarative view layer and perform a small imperative DOM action. Typical cases include:

  • moving focus to a particular element

  • reading or adjusting browser-managed selection or playback state

  • calling DOM or library APIs that operate on a concrete node

Prefer ordinary views, callbacks, and observables when the behavior can already be expressed declaratively.

#lang webracket
(define @input (@ #f))
 
(vpanel
 (Input #:ref @input)
 (Button "Focus input"
         (lambda ()
(define node (obs-peek @input))
(when node
  (js-send node "focus" (vector))))))

23.5.2 Autofocus🔗

Primitive elements accept a #:autofocus keyword argument. Components can also use #:autofocus when they forward root attributes to a primitive root element.

When #:autofocus is true, web-easy will focus the mounted root DOM node after it appears in the browser. This makes #:autofocus useful not only for initial page load, but also for dynamically mounted UI such as editors, dialogs, and popovers.

Use #:autofocus for the common declarative case where a newly mounted element should receive focus automatically. Use #:ref when you need lower-level control over exactly when or how focus is moved.

Components that forward root attributes can also forward #:ref and generic bubbling DOM event keywords such as #:on-keydown.

#lang webracket
(Input #:autofocus #t)
 
(Div #:tabindex 0
     #:autofocus #t
     "Keyboard focus starts here")

procedure

(event? evt) → boolean?

  evt : external
(mouse-event? evt) → boolean?
  evt : external
(keyboard-event? evt) → boolean?
  evt : external
(pointer-event? evt) → boolean?
  evt : external
(focus-event? evt) → boolean?
  evt : external
(input-event? evt) → boolean?
  evt : external
(submit-event? evt) → boolean?
  evt : external
(touch-event? evt) → boolean?
  evt : external
(wheel-event? evt) → boolean?
  evt : external
Check whether an external value contains a DOM event object of a particular kind.

The argument evt is an external value. These predicates check whether it contains a JavaScript Event, MouseEvent, KeyboardEvent, PointerEvent, FocusEvent, InputEvent, SubmitEvent, TouchEvent, or WheelEvent object, respectively.

procedure

(touch-list? v) → boolean?

  v : any/c
(touch? v) → boolean?
  v : any/c
Check whether a value is a browser touch collection or touch object.

touch-list? reports whether v is an external containing a JavaScript TouchList object.

touch? reports whether v is an external containing a JavaScript Touch object.

procedure

(event-type evt) → string?

  evt : external
(event-target evt) → (or/c #f external)
  evt : external
(event-current-target evt) → (or/c #f external)
  evt : external
Read common properties from a raw browser event object.

The argument evt is an external value expected to contain a JavaScript Event object.

event-type returns the DOM event type, such as "click" or "contextmenu".

event-target returns the event target object, if any.

event-current-target returns the object whose listener is currently running, if any.

procedure

(prevent-default! evt) → void?

  evt : external
(stop-propagation! evt) → void?

23.6 Theme🔗

web-easy also provides a small stylesheet-based theme API.

This API is intentionally concrete:

  • a theme value describes the root html class and CSS files to use

  • install-theme-manager! installs the stylesheet link nodes

  • set-theme! switches the active theme

  • observe-theme! keeps a theme manager in sync with an observable

The stylesheet load order is:

  • core CSS

  • theme CSS

  • optional extra/page CSS

The starter theme stylesheets use a small set of token tiers:

  • neutral/page tokens such as background, foreground, subtle surfaces, and separators

  • control and popup tokens for shared widget chrome

  • semantic base tones such as --we-primary and --we-success

  • semantic companion tokens for soft surfaces and readable accents: --we-*-subtle, --we-*-border, --we-*-emphasis, and --we-*-on

This keeps the starter themes approachable: most customization can happen by editing token values before changing component-specific selectors.

procedure

(theme id    
  class-name    
  core-css    
  theme-css    
  extra-css) → theme?
  id : any/c
  class-name : string?
  core-css : string?
  theme-css : string?
  extra-css : (or/c #f string?)
Create a browser theme descriptor.

The resulting value records:

  • id, an application-chosen theme identifier

  • class-name, the class applied to the root <html> element

  • core-css, the shared core stylesheet path

  • theme-css, the main theme stylesheet path

  • extra-css, an optional extra/page stylesheet path

procedure

(theme? v) → boolean?

  v : any/c
Report whether v is a theme descriptor.

procedure

(theme-manager? v) → boolean?

  v : any/c
Report whether v is a browser theme manager created by install-theme-manager!.

procedure

(install-theme-manager! initial-theme) → theme-manager?

  initial-theme : theme?
Install or reuse the managed stylesheet links in <head> and apply initial-theme immediately.

The managed link ids are:

  • we-theme-core-css

  • we-theme-css

  • we-theme-extra-css

procedure

(set-theme! manager next-theme) → void?

  manager : theme-manager?
  next-theme : theme?
Switch manager to next-theme.

This updates the root html theme class and the managed stylesheet href attributes.

procedure

(observe-theme! manager    
  theme    
  theme->descriptor) → void?
  manager : theme-manager?
  theme : obs?
  theme->descriptor : procedure?
Synchronize manager with the observable theme.

The procedure theme->descriptor is called on the current observable value and on each later update. It must return a theme value.

A common pattern is:

  • define one or more theme values

  • install a theme manager with the initial theme

  • optionally switch themes directly with set-theme!

  • or keep the manager in sync with an observable using observe-theme!

23.6.1 Theme Example🔗

#lang webracket
; Define two named themes that share the same core CSS.
(define light-theme
(theme 'light
       "we-theme-light"
       "web-easy-core.css"
       "theme-light.css"
       #f))
 
(define dark-theme
(theme 'dark
       "we-theme-dark"
       "web-easy-core.css"
       "theme-dark.css"
       #f))
 
; Install the stylesheet links and apply the initial theme.
(define tm
(install-theme-manager! light-theme))
 
; set-theme! uses the existing manager to switch to another theme.
(set-theme! tm dark-theme)
 
; Or controlled reactively from an observable.
(define @theme
(obs 'light))
 
(observe-theme! tm
                @theme
                (lambda (id)
       (case id
         [(light) light-theme]
         [(dark)  dark-theme]
         [else    light-theme])))

23.7 Core Primitives🔗

The uppercase HTML-like constructors and low-level HTML helpers form the core primitive API. They aim to mirror HTML semantics closely and provide the building blocks for higher-level component libraries.

23.7.1 Low-Level HTML Constructors🔗

The constructors below are low-level building blocks. Most users should prefer the uppercase primitive constructors (H1, P, Span, Div, and so on).

procedure

(html-element tag    
  content    
  [#:id id    
  #:class class    
  #:attrs attrs]) → view?
  tag : (or/c symbol? observable?)
  content : text-content/c
  id : (or/c #f string? symbol?) = #f
  class : any/c = #f
  attrs : html-attrs/c = null
Build a low-level primitive HTML leaf element from a tag and content.

Positional arguments: tag is the element tag (for example 'h1, 'p, 'span), and content is text-like content.

procedure

(html-element-children tag    
  [#:attrs attrs]    
  child ...) → view?
  tag : (or/c symbol? observable?)
  attrs : html-attrs/c = null
  child : view?
Build a low-level primitive HTML container element from a tag and child views.

Positional arguments: tag is the element tag (for example 'div, 'section), and each child is rendered as a child view.

Internal note: the related internal constructor observable-element-children supports an internal keyword #:after-render used by some compound components for backend bridging after child rebuilds. This hook is internal and not part of the public stability contract.

For dynamic tag use with html-element and html-element-children, tag changes are handled with remount semantics: when the tag changes, the underlying DOM node is replaced (similar to React/Angular element-type changes), rather than mutated in place. This means DOM identity can change across tag updates.

For internal component authoring in web-easy, define/component supports variadic children with #:rest, including together with #:root-attrs.

When a component uses #:root-attrs, the forwarded root keyword surface can include ordinary root attributes, #:ref, #:autofocus, and generic bubbling DOM event keywords named #:on-<dom-event-name>.

Internal status note: built-in semantic/compound constructors are implemented with define/component; only html-element, html-element-children, and internal observable-element-children remain on define/key.

#lang webracket
(define/component Example
#:root-tag 'div
#:rest children
#:root-attrs attrs/final
(define attrs/final
(list (cons 'class "example")))
(apply Div
       (append children
               (list #:attrs attrs/final))))

23.7.2 Primitive HTML Elements🔗

The uppercase constructors below map directly to primitive HTML elements. They accept:

  • content as text/observable content

  • #:attrs as an optional attribute list matching html-attrs/c

  • keyword attributes corresponding to HTML attributes for the specific element (plus global attributes and data-*/aria-*)

  • generic bubbling DOM event keywords named #:on-<dom-event-name>

Attribute-list entries in #:attrs must match html-attr-entry/c.

Example:

#lang webracket
(H1 "Title"
    #:attrs '((id "hero")
              (title "Welcome")
              (class "big")))

Even though the signatures below list #:attrs, direct keyword attributes are also available for all allowed HTML attributes (global + element-specific + data-*/aria-*).

Example:

#lang webracket
(H1 "Title"
    #:id "hero"
    #:lang "en"
    #:title "Welcome"
    #:data-testid "hero-1"
    #:aria-label "Main heading")

Unknown keyword attributes are rejected, and observable attribute values are supported. Primitive DOM event callbacks receive the raw browser event object.

Example with direct keywords and #:attrs:

#lang webracket
(window
 (container
  (H1 "Profile"
      #:id "profile-title"
      #:lang "en"
      #:attrs '((data-testid "title-1")))
(P "Welcome to the profile page."
   #:class "lead")
(Span "beta"
      #:attrs '((aria-label "beta label")
                (style "font-style: italic;")))))

In this section, leaf means the constructor takes one content value and produces a single HTML node (as opposed to container-style constructors that are built from child view arguments).

Within each subsection below, constructors are listed alphabetically.

23.7.3 Text and Inline Elements🔗

#lang webracket

 #:width 400
 #:height 300
 #:on-mouseup
 (lambda (evt)
(define x (js-ref/extern evt "offsetX"))
(define y (js-ref/extern evt "offsetY"))
(js-log (format "mouse up at (~a, ~a)" x y)))
(Span "Canvas fallback"))

procedure

(menu-popup item    
  ...    
  [#:left left    
  #:top top    
  #:position position    
  #:z-index z-index]) → view?
  item : view?
  left : (or/c #f real? string?) = #f
  top : (or/c #f real? string?) = #f
  position : (or/c #f symbol? string?) = #f
  z-index : (or/c #f real? string?) = #f
Build a standalone popup menu container.

Positional arguments: each item is usually a menu-item or divider. This constructor also accepts global HTML keyword attributes for its root <vpanel> element.

Optional positioning keywords: #:left and #:top place the popup explicitly; numeric values are rendered in pixels. #:position overrides the CSS positioning mode and defaults to 'absolute when any explicit positioning keyword is used. #:z-index sets popup stacking order.

When #:position is 'absolute (the default for explicitly positioned popups), #:left and #:top are interpreted in the same way as CSS absolute positioning: they are relative to the popup’s containing block, which is usually the nearest positioned ancestor. In practice, this means standalone context menus are often rendered inside a wrapper with position: relative, and the popup offsets are measured from that wrapper’s top-left corner.

Example:

#lang webracket
(Div #:style "position: relative;"
     (Canvas #:id "circle-canvas")
     (menu-popup
      #:left 120
      #:top 80
      #:z-index 1000
      (menu-item "Delete" (lambda () (void)))))

The browser backend gives standalone popup menus menu-style keyboard behavior:

ArrowDown and Home enter the popup at the first item. ArrowUp and End enter the popup at the last item. Typing a letter performs type-ahead focus. Closing the popup returns focus to the element that was focused before the popup opened.
